questions.q: From where did Laban and his sons believe Jacob had gotten all his wealth?
questions.a: Laban and his sons believed that Jacob had gotten all his wealth from Laban’s possessions.

questions.q: What instructions did Yahweh give Jacob?
questions.a: Yahweh instructed Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and to his relatives.

questions.q: How had God taken away the cattle of Laban and given them to Jacob?
questions.a: God had caused the animals to bear speckled and striped young, which were Jacob’s wages.

questions.q: What attitude did Rachel and Leah have toward their father Laban?
questions.a: Rachel and Leah said that Laban treated them as foreigners and had devoured their money.

questions.q: What did Rachel do before leaving with Jacob?
questions.a: Rachel stole her father’s household gods.

questions.q: How did Jacob deceive Laban at this time?
questions.a: Jacob deceived Laban by not telling Laban that he was leaving.

questions.q: What did Laban do when he was told that Jacob had fled?
questions.a: Laban took his relatives with him and pursued Jacob, overtaking him after seven days.

questions.q: What did God tell Laban in a dream?
questions.a: God told Laban to speak neither good or bad to Jacob.

questions.q: Why did Jacob say that he had fled from Laban secretly?
questions.a: Jacob said that he fled secretly because he was afraid that Laban would take his daughters from him by force.

questions.q: What did Jacob say when Laban accused him of stealing his household gods?
questions.a: Jacob said that whoever stole Laban’s household gods would not continue to live.

questions.q: Why did Laban not find his household gods among Jacob’s possessions?
questions.a: Laban did not find his household gods because Rachel sat on them and then said that she could not stand up since she was having her period.

questions.q: How long had Jacob worked for Laban, and how many times had Laban changed his wages?
questions.a: Jacob had worked for Laban twenty years, and Laban had changed his wages ten times.

questions.q: How did Laban show that he still thought of Jacob’s possessions as his own?
questions.a: Laban said that all that he saw of Jacob’s possessions was his.

questions.q: How did Jacob and Laban mark the place of their covenant?
questions.a: Jacob and Laban marked the place of their covenant by making a pile of stones there.

questions.q: Who was declared as witness between Jacob and Laban to ensure the covenant would be kept?
questions.a: God was declared as witness between Jacob and Laban to ensure that the covenant would be kept.

questions.q: What were the pile and the pillar for?
questions.a: The pile and pillar were both witnesses to the covenant, which said that neither Laban nor Jacob would pass the pile or pillar to do one another harm.

questions.q: What covenant did Jacob and Laban make?
questions.a: Jacob and Laban each agreed to not pass beyond the pile of stones to do the other harm.

questions.q: What did Jacob do to show that he agreed to the covenant?
questions.a: To show that he agreed with Laban about the covenant, Jacob swore by God, whom his father Isaac feared.

questions.q: What did Laban do the next morning?
questions.a: Laban rose, kissed his grandchildren and daughters, blessed them, and returned home.

commentary.text: Verses 1–21 The affairs of these families are related very minutely, while (what are called) the great events of states and kingdoms at that period, are not mentioned. The Bible teaches people the common duties of life, how to serve God, how to enjoy the blessings he bestows, and to do good in the various stations and duties of life. Selfish men consider themselves robbed of all that goes past them, and covetousness will even swallow up natural affection. Men's overvaluing worldly wealth is that error which is the root of covetousness, envy, and all evil. The men of the world stand in each other's way, and every one seems to be taking away from the rest; hence discontent, envy, and discord. But there are possessions that will suffice for all; happy they who seek them in the first place. In all our removals we should have respect to the command and promise of God. If He be with us, we need not fear. The perils which surround us are so many, that nothing else can really encourage our hearts. To remember favoured seasons of communion with God, is very refreshing when in difficulties; and we should often recollect our vows, that we fail not to fulfil them.

God can put a bridle in the mouth of wicked men, to restrain their malice, though he do not change their hearts. Though they have no love to God's people, they will pretend to it, and try to make a merit of necessity. Foolish Laban! to call those things his gods which could be stolen! Enemies may steal our goods, but not our God. Here Laban lays to Jacob's charge things that he knew not. Those who commit their cause to God, are not forbidden to plead it themselves with meekness and fear. When we read of Rachel's stealing her father's images, what a scene of iniquity opens! The family of Nahor, who left the idolatrous Chaldees; is this family itself become idolatrous? It is even so. The truth seems to be, that they were like some in after-times, who sware by the Lord and by Malcham, Zep 1:5; and like others in our times, who wish to serve both God and mammon. Great numbers will acknowledge the true God in words, but their hearts and houses are the abodes of spiritual idolatry. When a man gives himself up to covetousness, like Laban, the world is his god; and he has only to reside among gross idolaters in order to become one, or at least a favourer of their abominations.

If Jacob were willingly consumed with heat in the day, and frost by night, to become the son-in-law of Laban, what should we refuse to endure, to become the sons of God? Jacob speaks of God as the God of his father; he thought himself unworthy to be regarded, but was beloved for his father's sake. He calls him the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac; for Abraham was dead, and gone to that world where perfect love casts out fear; but Isaac was yet alive, sanctifying the Lord in his heart, as his fear and his dread.

Laban could neither justify himself nor condemn Jacob, therefore desires to hear no more of that matter. He is not willing to own himself in fault, as he ought to have done. But he proposes a covenant of friendship between them, to which Jacob readily agrees. A heap of stones was raised, to keep up the memory of the event, writing being then not known or little used. A sacrifice of peace offerings was offered. Peace with God puts true comfort into our peace with our friends. They did eat bread together, partaking of the feast upon the sacrifice. In ancient times covenants of friendship were ratified by the parties eating and drinking together. God is judge between contending parties, and he will judge righteously; whoever do wrong, it is at their peril. They gave a new name to the place, The heap of witness. After this angry parley, they part friends. God is often better to us than our fears, and overrules the spirits of men in our favour, beyond what we could have expected; for it is not in vain to trust in him.
